transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Amy Held.
Candidates are making their final push this weekend before Tuesday's midterm election.
President Trump making the case for Republicans with telerallies today.
Polling, ad money, plus candidate and surrogate travel all indicate competitive races in places
Trump won by double digits in 2024.
Meantime, early voting has set a record with more than 50 million Americans casting their
ballots so far.
Cost of living is the top issue, with a third of people saying they've experienced economic
hardship over the past year.
That's according to a new NPR/PBS News Marist poll.
Also on track to set a record, campaign spending.
These midterms will likely be the most expensive on record.
NPR's Ron Elving reports Democrats have been outspent in almost every race.
They're battling almost limitless resources from Republican donors such as Elon Musk.
Multiple sources say that he has spent over $350 million on this cycle overall.
So the Democrats hope that voters will still be able to get information.
That's NPR's Ron Elving reporting.
A federal judge has dismissed Trump's lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal.
As NPR's Stephen Bizaha reports, it involves a birthday card Trump allegedly sent to the
late convicted sex offender, Jeffrey Epstein.
The letter included a drawing of a naked woman and what appeared to be the president's signature.
The journal reported this in July last year.
Trump denied anything to do with the letter and called the journal's story fake and sued
for at least $10 billion in damages.
The federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, declining to rule on whether the actual reporting was
false, and saying the president had failed to show the journal had acted with actual
malice.
This is the second time Trump has tried to sue the Wall Street Journal over this reporting.
The latest case was dismissed with prejudice, preventing Trump from filing another lawsuit.
Stephen Bizaha, NPR News, Birmingham, Alabama.
Iran's Supreme Leader says his country will respond forcefully if anyone attacks, according
to state media.
This, as the U.S. and Israel say, they are preparing for a potential return to hostilities
after the midterm elections next week.
NPR's Hadil El-Shelchi reports.
Ayatollah Mushta Bachamane said that, quote, "any level or type of threat to Iran" would
face a, quote, "immediate and impactful response."
The Supreme Leader made the comments in a meeting with Iranian military officials, according
to Iranian state media.
He also ordered the military to update their attack plans with U.S. and Israeli targets.
This comes at a time when Iran has intensified its attacks on ships trying to cross the Strait
of Hormuz.
According to Iranian state media, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said that on Friday,
four tankers, one of which was carrying two million barrels of oil, caught fire after
hitting mines in the strait.
Hadil El-Shelchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
It's NPR News.
This is the real sugar high, candy prices up around 8 percent over last Halloween, according
to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
And compared to 2020, they've risen almost 50 percent.
Some of it is due to tariffs and climate factors that have hurt cocoa harvests.
It's a new day for four people in Texas who spent 378 days at the NASA Johnson Space Center
living like they were on Mars.
Today, they left the simulation space for the first time since entering, Michael Atkinson
from Houston Public Media reports.
The crew felt the sun for the first time since last year, as their friends and family cheered
them on.
They've been living in a 1,700-square-foot, 3D-printed living space, growing crops, studying
geology, and even experiencing simulated communications delays with mission control.
Ross Elder served as mission commander.
The risks are great, but through seeking understanding, strong vision and leadership, creativity,
fortitude, hard work, and an incredible foundation, the goal of putting humans on Mars is not
only achievable, but rather inevitable.
NASA says the simulation will help the agency study how humans could handle a future real-life
Mars mission.
I'm Michael Atkinson in Houston.
Its legs are small, but its reach is large.
The Dachshund, an icon off the leech, is a new art exhibition opening in Germany today,
the artwork inspired by the animal known as a sausage dog, including by famous fans Pablo
Picasso and Andy Warhol.
Organizers say there will even be time for Dachshunds themselves to come by for a look
and a sniff.
It's NPR News.

topics.text: Candidates make final push before Tuesday's midterm elections; early voting tops 50 million
NPR/PBS News Marist poll finds cost of living is top midterm issue
Midterm campaign spending on track to be the most expensive on record, Musk spending heavily
Federal judge dismisses Trump's lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter
Iran's Supreme Leader vows forceful response to any attack, orders military to update attack plans
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says four tankers caught fire after hitting mines in Strait of Hormuz
Candy prices up about 8 percent over last year, nearly 50 percent since 2020, per Bureau of Labor Statistics
Four crew members emerge from 378-day NASA Mars simulation at Johnson Space Center in Houston
Dachshund art exhibition opens in Germany featuring works inspired by the sausage dog
